Name: Leah
Transcript: Thanks for doing this. There are no right or wrong answers, it's your experience I'm interested in, and we can stop whenever you like. So, to start. Can you tell me how you came to be working from home, and what it's like for you now?

Name: Dev
Transcript: Sure. So I'm a software tester, for a bank. Testing the app, the online banking, making sure when you press a button it does what it says. And we were in an office in Canary Wharf, and in 2020 they sent everyone home, and then they sort of discovered they could save a fortune on floors. So they got rid of most of the building. You can still go in, but there's about forty desks for six hundred people, and you have to book. So I'm home most of the time. And at first I loved it. I really did. No Jubilee line, no sweaty platform. I thought, this is the dream. And it's, I don't know. Six years in, I'm less sure.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Less sure. What's changed?

Name: Dev
Transcript: I think I've changed. Or it's changed me, maybe. I used to have this whole other life in the office. I had my desk, I had my mug, I had my lunch place. I was Dev from testing. People knew me. And now I'm just, I'm in the flat. The same flat I sleep in and eat in and argue about the bins in. And I think I've sort of shrunk to fit it.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Shrunk to fit it. What's that like?

Name: Dev
Transcript: Small. It's like, some weeks I don't leave the flat apart from the walk round the block and the big Tesco on a Saturday. And I don't notice, that's the thing. I don't notice until Sam says, when did you last go out, properly. And I have to think about it. And on Teams all anyone sees of me is my face and the kitchen cupboards behind me. I tidied the bit behind me for about a year. Moved the fruit bowl, put the washing-up away before a call. Like my kitchen was going to be marked. I've stopped now, mostly. But I still check what's behind me before I turn the camera on.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Can you take me through a normal working day, from when you get up?

Name: Dev
Transcript: So Sam, my partner, she's a dental nurse, so she leaves at about half seven. And I'll get up when she goes. And I'll do the thing, I've got this thing where I go out the front door, walk round the block, and come back in. Ten minutes. I read about it, the fake commute. And it does help, actually. It's daft, but I walk out of my front door as a man in a flat, and I walk back in as, you know, someone at work. Then I'm at the kitchen table by eight. And it's tickets, test runs, stand-up at half nine on Teams. And then, honestly, I tend to just keep going. Lunch at the laptop. I look up and it's six, and Sam's back, and I haven't moved.

Name: Leah
Transcript: You haven't moved.

Name: Dev
Transcript: No. I work longer now than I ever did in the office. Way longer. And I've thought about why. And I think it's, in the office, there was an end. Everyone packed up at half five and you'd feel weird being the last one. At home, there's nobody packing up. And there's this feeling, I don't know if you get it, that because I'm at home, I should be doing more. Like, I've saved an hour and a half on the commute, so the bank's owed that hour and a half. Nobody's asked for it. I just give it.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Where in your home do you work? What's that space like for you?

Name: Dev
Transcript: The kitchen table. It's a one-bed flat, so there's nowhere else. The kitchen's sort of part of the living room. So the sofa is about two metres from my desk, basically. And I think that's the hardest bit, if I'm honest. There's no room in the flat that's just home. When I sit on the sofa in the evening, I can see the table, and I can see the laptop, and it's like the office is watching me. Sam bought me this, like a big wicker basket. And at the end of the day the laptop and the keyboard and the headset go in the basket and the lid goes on and the basket goes under the table. And then it's a kitchen table again.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What's that like, putting it in the basket?

Name: Dev
Transcript: When I do it, it's good. It's like a full stop. The trouble is I don't always do it. If there's a release going out, I'll leave it out, just in case. And then it's out for a week.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What happens at the start and the end of your working day?

Name: Dev
Transcript: Started is the walk round the block. That's quite clear. Finished, I'd say, finished is when Sam comes in. Which isn't great, because it means it's her key in the door that tells me to stop. Not me. And on her late days, it's half seven, eight o'clock before I stop. She said to me a while ago, you're not working from home, you're living at work. And she was right, and I was quite hurt by it, because she was right.

Name: Leah
Transcript: How has working from home changed things with the people you live with, or the people around you?

Name: Dev
Transcript: Sam, obviously. So she goes out to work, and I'm at home. And there's a thing that's crept in where the house stuff is mine. Because I'm here. I'll put a wash on at lunchtime, I'll do the hoovering in a quiet bit, I'll be in for deliveries, I'll sort the bins. And that's fine, it's fair, in a way. But it's also, it's not counted. It happens in the gaps, so it doesn't look like anything. She comes home and the flat's tidy and she's tired from her day, and my day was at home, so it can't have been that tiring. That's sort of the feeling. Not that she says that. But that's the feeling in the room.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What do you do with that feeling in the room?

Name: Dev
Transcript: Mostly I swallow it. Sometimes it comes out sideways. We had a row about the bins a while back, a proper one, and it wasn't about the bins. It was about, I've done the bins and the washing and the shopping and a full day's work, and none of it shows. And she was upset because she'd been on her feet all day with patients, and she's right, that's hard, that's harder than what I do. So then I felt bad for even saying it. I think that's where it always ends up. My day doesn't sound like much when you say it out loud.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Can you tell me about a day working from home that has stayed with you?

Name: Dev
Transcript: The neighbour upstairs had their bathroom done last spring. Three weeks of drilling. And I had a big release, a go-live, and I was on calls all day with the developers, and every few minutes this drill would go through the ceiling. And in an office, if the building's noisy, it's the building's problem. At home, it's somehow my problem. Like I should have a quieter flat. I ended up going to my mum's in Ilford for a week, and working in my old bedroom. Thirty-four years old. Next to my old posters.

Name: Leah
Transcript: What, if anything, do you miss about working somewhere else? And what would you miss if you had to go back?

Name: Dev
Transcript: I miss being someone at work. I don't know how else to say it. I had my work shirts. I'd iron them on a Sunday night. And I'd put one on and I was, I was that person, I was quite good at being that person. Quite funny. People would come to my desk with a question and stay for ten minutes. Now I'm in a t-shirt and nobody comes to my desk because my desk is my kitchen. And on Teams you can't really be funny, you just come across as a bit much. And the lunches. There was a little Turkish place, and three or four of us would go on a Friday. I miss that a lot. What would I miss if I went back? Not the Jubilee line. I'd miss being here when Sam gets home, I suppose. Seeing her first. Even if I'm still on the laptop.

Name: Leah
Transcript: Is there anything about working from home that we haven't touched on, that matters to you?

Name: Dev
Transcript: Maybe just that it looked like freedom. At the start. And there's a lot of freedom in it, I can do the washing whenever I like. But I think I've lost a bit of myself in the flat. And I don't know how to get it back without getting on the Jubilee line, which I really don't want to do. And I can't really say any of this to anyone. My brother drives a van, he's out at five. If I said I was finding it hard working from home, he'd laugh at me.
